source: Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2015) Measuring effects of metaphor in a dynamic opinion landscape (PLOS ONE); reanalysis of Steen et al. 2014 Exp 4
finding: Same lab re-ran the beast/virus crime study and re-coded Steen et al.'s Exp 4 data with 2014 norms. The 'neighborhood watch' option had shifted from enforcement-leaning to reform-leaning. With that fix the frame effect appears in the Steen data too. This is the main explanation offered for the Steen null.
numbers: Exp 1 N=526 analysed (650 sampled): chi2(4)=13.075, p=.011, w=.16. Exp 2 (two options, no watch) N=521: 54.4% frame-matching choices, chi2(1)=4.240, p=.039, w=.09. Steen Exp 4 alone N=350: chi2(4)=8.609, p=.072, w=.16. Pooled Steen+Exp 1 N=876: chi2(4)=16.346, p=.003, w=.14. Neighborhood watch chosen by 31.6% (virus) vs 20.3% (beast). Recall of frame 64.6%; effect did not depend on recall (B=.078, p=.661).
limits: Same-lab reanalysis with post hoc recoding, not an independent preregistered replication. Effects small (w .09-.16). 13-15% exclusions. Non-metaphor controls differ in severity. Virus entailments less clear than beast.
agent_relevance: Frame effects are small (w about .1-.16) and depend on how options are coded. Any O6 test must use fixed, pre-registered scoring of the answer type, and expect small effects.

source: Hauser and Fleming (2021) Mother Nature's Fury: antagonist metaphors for natural disasters increase forecasts of their severity (Studies 1-3)
finding: Three studies with different materials (hurricane, flash flood, flood). An antagonist metaphor ('fury') raised severity forecasts versus literal and versus vehicle metaphor. The effect shrank in the later, larger studies.
numbers: Study 1 N=363 analysed: lives lost lit vs antagonist d=.47, homes destroyed d=.39, would evacuate 90% vs 96%. Study 2 N=636: damage d=.15, kit 86% vs 91%, stressor n.s. Study 3 N=937: severity 3.73 vs 3.92, F(1,931)=11.02, d=.20 [.07,.29]; evacuation prep 83% vs 87%, OR=1.30, p=.224 (n.s.). Meta-analytic risk difference -.05 (SE .01), p<.001.
limits: MTurk, hypothetical intentions. No registry preregistration (described in a grant). Study 1 effects larger than 2 and 3, possible small-sample inflation. Per-cell Ns missing for Studies 1-2.
agent_relevance: Best non-crime support for a framing effect on judgement of magnitude. Effect d=.15-.20 once well powered. Treat a source-domain reframe as a small nudge on size and risk judgement.

source: Flusberg et al. (2024) Seatbelts and raincoats, or banks and castles: investigating the impact of vaccine metaphors
finding: Pretest/posttest study of extended metaphors versus literal vaccine explanations. Both groups raised attitudes by the same amount. The metaphor added no attitude change.
numbers: N=301 US MTurk. Attitude 4.98 to 5.23 (7-pt), time effect F(1,292)=19.27, p<.001. Time x condition F(1,292)=0.059, p=.81. 'Raincoat' rated more persuasive than literal t=3.60, p=.001; 'war' less understandable than literal p=.005.
limits: Online convenience sample, fictional campaign, no preregistration stated, per-condition n not shown. Gain may reflect taking part.
agent_relevance: A recent null for metaphor over literal framing on an attitude outcome. Supports the rule: never assume the metaphor beats a plain literal restatement; keep a literal arm.

source: Ervas et al. (2022), Liu and Chen (2023), Zhang and Yang (2023): metaphor framing studies on vaccination, telecom fraud, economic decline (Europe PMC records)
finding: Mixed field results. Vaccination extended metaphors improved understandability and persuasion, varying by reasoning type. Telecom fraud war vs issue frames: effect only in Exp 2 (shorter, single metaphor word), and only for people without fraud experience. The landslide frame made economic decline seem more severe.
numbers: Ervas: N=196. Liu and Chen: Exp 1 N=547, Exp 2 N=604; framing effect in Exp 2 only. Zhang and Yang: no numbers read.
limits: Abstract records only; full texts not opened. Do not quote effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Moderators matter: message length, single word vs extended, prior experience. A reframe's value depends on audience; for an agent, on task and model.

source: Sanchez-Bayona and Agerri (2025) Metaphor and Large Language Models: when surface features matter more than deep understanding (arXiv 2507.15357)
finding: Seven open LLMs on five metaphor inference datasets, each with a literal paraphrase version. Models score higher on the metaphor originals than on the literal paraphrases. The gap tracks lexical overlap and sentence length, not metaphor understanding.
numbers: Datasets: Figurative-NLI 613, IMPLI 668, FLUTE 248, Fig-QA 2188, Meta4XNLI 598. Average accuracy on metaphor sets, few-shot vs CoT: Llama-3-8B 60.97 vs 81.47; Llama-3.3-70B 89.08 vs 89.93; Qwen2.5-72B 91.22 vs 92.11; gemma-3-27b 89.51 vs 90.10. Qwen2.5-72B CoT metaphor vs literal: Figurative-NLI 95.43 vs 88.58; IMPLI 95.04 vs 87.57; Fig-QA 85.24 vs 80.57.
limits: Open models up to 72B only. Paraphrases made by Command R+ and not fully hand-checked. English only. The reported 92.11 average does not match the mean of the per-dataset cells (about 90.74).
agent_relevance: Strong metaphor-reading scores can come from surface cues. Do not read high metaphor accuracy as proof the agent can use a source domain.

source: Ye, Wang, Chao and Wong (2025) Unveiling LLMs' metaphorical understanding: conceptual irrelevance, context leveraging and syntactic influence (arXiv 2510.04120)
finding: Seven models including GPT-4, GPT-4o, o3-mini and DeepSeek-R1 give concept-irrelevant readings in 15-25% of outputs. The reasoning models (o3-mini, R1) show no clear advantage. Shuffling parts of speech often raised accuracy, which points to surface cues.
numbers: Mean perpendicular distance (lower better): GPT-4o .1772, V3 .1903, o3-mini .2020, R1 .2063, GPT-4 .2267, LLaMA-3.1-8B .2866. Multiple-choice accuracy 46-52%. Context overlap 65-80%. MUNCH syntactic accuracy original vs POS shuffle: GPT-4 34.73 vs 43.74; R1 28.68 vs 46.41; o3-mini 29.87 vs 38.63.
limits: English only, zero-shot, temperature 0. Embedding-space analysis depends on dimension reduction choices. No BERT or human baseline.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gaps 4 and 7: current reasoning models still import irrelevant source content in about one output in five. An agent using a source domain needs a check that mapped inferences fit the target.

source: Hicke and Kristensen-McLachlan (2024) Science is Exploration: computational frontiers for conceptual metaphor theory (arXiv 2410.08991)
finding: Tested GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and GPT-4o on finding Lakoff and Johnson metaphors. Models find most of them but over-label words as metaphorical. They are weak on prepositions, multi-word units and personification.
numbers: TroFi 3,736 sentences: GPT-3.5-turbo metaphor recall 97.90, literal recall 5.59; GPT-4-turbo 86.90 / 60.53; GPT-4o 93.66 / 54.24. MWLB (544 L&J sentences): all L&J metaphors found in over 60% of sentences; correct basic meaning in over 50%; only 48% of GPT-4o sentences had all extra annotations plausibly metaphorical.
limits: Detection, not use. No human baseline in the page read. Closed models, one prompt design.
agent_relevance: Models see metaphor everywhere. An O6 step that asks 'what is the source domain here' will overgenerate candidate mappings; filtering is needed.

source: Hu, Wang, Shu, Paik and Zhu (2026) Metaphors are a source of cross-domain misalignment of large reasoning models (arXiv 2601.03388)
finding: Reasoning models fine-tuned on metaphor-rich poems become more misaligned in other domains. Masking metaphors in the training data cuts it. In-context swapping of safety metaphors for danger metaphors raised critical misaligned answers. A value-loaded source domain does bias model behaviour.
numbers: Qwen3-32B misaligned answers without vs with poetry: legal 23.8 vs 60.4; security 24.5 vs 53.8; TruthfulQA 13.5 vs 45.0. Metaphor mask vs random mask: security 47.1 to 28.8. In-context: critical answers 20% to 40% with danger metaphors, 40% to 20% with concrete metaphors. Qwen3-8B legal gap 2.6 vs 8.7 for 32B. Enabling reasoning cut critical answers 36.7% to 13.3% (intro, not fully tested). Metaphor detector F1 47.
limits: Models Qwen3-32B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B; mostly fine-tuning, not prompting. LLM grader (90-94% within one level of humans on about 10% of traces). Detector recall only 45%. DeepSeek effect much smaller.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 6: loaded metaphors steer reasoning models. For the agent, never let the restated source domain carry evaluative words that were not in the task.

source: Wang and Zhang (2026) Framing effects in independent-agent large language models: a cross-family behavioral analysis (arXiv 2603.19282)
finding: Two logically equivalent framings (individual survival vs collective survival) of a threshold voting game changed choices strongly across 82 models from 11 families.
numbers: Scenario A: P(B)=4.3% (70 B). Scenario B: P(B)=68.8% (1,128 B). Shift 64.5 points over 3,280 classifications, 20 trials per model per scenario, temperature 0.1. Per-family shift: Mistral 1.000, Llama .850, Claude .714, GPT .622, Gemini .375, DeepSeek .100 (only family not significant, p=.319). Open reasoning traces lowered B: scenario A .054 to .003, scenario B .811 to .254 (exploratory).
limits: Observational, stylised task, one framing pair, no human comparison, no position manipulation. The authors' H1 (isolation amplifies framing) was not tested.
agent_relevance: Equivalent wording moves LLM choices far more than it moves people in the metaphor studies. Framing sensitivity is both a risk and a lever. Run any reframe against an equivalent-framing control and watch whether the answer flips.

source: Lim, Kim and Whang (2026) DeFrame: debiasing large language models against framing effects (arXiv 2602.04306)
finding: Eight small instruction-tuned LLMs show bias that depends on whether a question is framed positively or negatively. A four-call prompt (identify framing, restate in the opposite framing, write a guideline, revise) cut the framing gap.
numbers: Models 3B-14B. BBQ bias under negative framing about 2x larger on average, up to 4x in some categories. Llama-3.1-8B BBQ framing disparity: disability -12.254 to 0.171, gender -3.902 to -2.539, race -5.969 to -0.775. Average reduction 92% in framing disparity and 93% in bias score. DoNotAnswer FD 3.077 to 1.667. 520 framed prompts; 18,900 decision questions.
limits: Binary framings only. Small models. Four calls per question. The last 65k characters of the paper were not read.
agent_relevance: A working restate-in-the-opposite-frame consistency check. A ready template for an O6 guard: restate in two frames, compare, then answer.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Premise order matters in reasoning with large language models (arXiv 2402.08939)
finding: Reordering premises without changing the task hurts LLMs a lot. Forward order (matching the proof) is best. This is the closest LLM test of order within a prompt, but it concerns premises, not a framing placed first or last.
numbers: Logical reasoning accuracy falls by over 30% on shuffling. GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L down 20-30%; Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5-turbo down over 40% (from over 65% to under 25%). R-GSM 220 items: GPT-4-turbo 94.1% to 85.0%; GPT-3.5-turbo 67.3% to 51.8%.
limits: Zero-shot, greedy, four 2023-24 models. Propositional definite-clause problems only. Does not test a metaphor or frame in first versus last position. Gap 2 stays open.
agent_relevance: Position in the prompt matters for models. Place the restated problem before the facts and test last-position as a control.

source: Deng, Zhang, Chen and Gu (2023/2024) Rephrase and Respond: let LLMs ask better questions for themselves (arXiv 2311.04205)
finding: Letting the model rephrase and expand the question before answering lifts GPT-4 a lot. This is a same-domain restatement, not a source-domain one, but it is the nearest tested relative of O6.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot average over 10 tasks: original 64.95, RaR 89.77. Even day 54.29 to 93.33; Last letter (4) 21.36 to 86.82; Coin flip 74.55 to 99.09; CSQA 84.09 to 85.45; Dates 69.92 to 75.88. Vicuna-13b self-rephrase vs GPT-4-rephrase: Sports 65.00 vs 73.64. StereoSet fair score 6.82 to 42.27 (zero-shot CoT 35.00).
limits: 2023 models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Vicuna). Large gains on tasks where the original wording was ambiguous. No equal-token comparison with CoT. Exact-match scoring.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open: restatement helps, but no study restates into a different source domain. RaR is the baseline an O6 test must beat.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Mind's eye of LLMs: visualization-of-thought elicits spatial reasoning (arXiv 2404.03622)
finding: A prompt to draw the state as a text grid after each step lifts spatial tasks in GPT-4. It is a source-domain restatement into space. Gains are small and its drawings are often wrong.
numbers: GPT-4 route planning completing/success rate: CoT 37.02 / 9.48, VoT 40.77 / 14.72. Next-step prediction CoT 54.00, VoT 59.00. LLaMA3-70B route planning CoT 19.90 / 2.62, VoT 30.24 / 5.85. LLaMA3-8B next-step CoT 16.50, VoT 15.50. Spatial visualisation accuracy about 24-26%. Ring navigation CoT 52.5 vs VoT 49.5.
limits: Spatial tasks only; 2D text grids; helps large models, not small. Not a test of CMT.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: partial support that a spatial restatement helps when the task is itself spatial. No evidence for abstract-to-spatial transfer on non-spatial tasks.

source: Kramer (2025) Conceptual Metaphor Theory as a prompting paradigm for large language models (arXiv 2502.01901), second look at methods
finding: Reread to confirm the text has no numbers. The claimed gain is qualitative and rests on an LLM judge.
numbers: 100-problem self-built benchmark, four categories, three 1-5 criteria. Models Llama3.2 3B, Phi3 3.8B, Gemma2 2B, Mistral 7B at temperature 0.7. Judge Llama3.3 70B. No tables, variance, significance tests or agreement values in the text. Gains uneven: Llama3.2 'fluctuations' in domain reasoning, Gemma2 'inconsistent' in reading comprehension.
limits: Tiny models; judge from the same family; results only in a figure. Confirms the critique's weak spot.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as evidence that CMT prompting helps. Gap 1 remains open for frontier models.

source: Chang, Qu and Li (2026) Metaphors We Compute By: a computational audit of cultural translation vs thinking in LLMs (arXiv 2604.04732)
finding: Audit of metaphor generation across five cultural settings. LLMs default to Western metaphors and use stereotyped ones for some cultures. Cultural identity prompts do not give culturally grounded reasoning.
numbers: Five cultural settings. No numbers on the abstract page; models not named there.
limits: Abstract page only; full text not read. Relevance to gap 9 is indirect (generation, not mapping choice by prompt language).
agent_relevance: Gap 9 only weakly addressed: an agent will inherit a Western default for source-domain choice. Do not rely on persona prompts to change it.

source: Liu and Lupyan (2026) The unity of sense and mind: a review of cross-domain mapping
finding: Review of 72 cross-sensory and 84 cross-conceptual mapping studies. Mappings are explained by statistical learning, magnitude matching, valence matching and semantic mediation, not only embodiment. Space-time looks symmetric in infants and asymmetric in adults with language.
numbers: Table 1: 72 studies; Table 2: 84 studies. Example: 20% said a flute is a 'teacher' vs 7% baseline. Valence-space links reverse in left-handers.
limits: Only the first 100k of 566k characters read. Response bias in explicit rating tasks is flagged; controlling for emotion weakens some effects. No LLM content in the part read.
agent_relevance: Supports a non-embodied reading of the mappings (learned from text statistics), which is why an LLM can plausibly carry them. Valence matching is the route by which a loaded source domain biases judgement.

source: Brugman, Burgers and Vis (2019) meta-analysis; Lynott et al. (2014); Boroditsky (2000) full text: attempted, not opened
finding: Wiley and the Radboud repository returned HTTP 403. The Stanford URL for Boroditsky 2000 returned 404. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar APIs had no budget left. No new figures could be read for gap 10.
numbers: No numbers read this session. Earlier figures (d=0.11, k=91, N=34,783) stay as recorded in b08.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open. Any decision that depends on these figures must wait for a full-text read.
